text:
(Continued)
UNITED STATES · PLANNING GUIDE FOR HOW TO DESIGN & CONSTRUCT:  The new "Forge-350" nuclear plant which is economical and meets current NRC requirements.

The building is a confinement structure for salt aerosols and tritium, not a 60-psig large-dry containment sized for a blowdown. This claim is already the Kairos licensing theory; Forge-350 should adopt it only to the extent Hermes data and the KP-BISON fuel methods support it.
• No large-break LOCA. Primary pressure under 2 bar and a boiling margin of several hundred degrees remove the accident that sizes light-water emergency core cooling. The replacement design-basis events are loss of forced flow, loss of heat sink, salt spill, air ingress into cover gas, and pebble-handling faults.
• Passive decay heat. Direct reactor auxiliary cooling to ambient air, natural circulation, no AC power and no operator action credited for 72 hours, with analysis carried to a stable end state beyond 72 hours. This matches what U.S. reviewers already accept on AP1000 and ESBWR, translated to salt.
• Reactivity. Negative temperature feedback from fuel and moderator. Voiding of salt is a case to analyze, not a
coefficient to assume. Shutdown uses absorbing blades or rods inserted by gravity, with a diverse second means.
• Source term and emergency planning. The design target is a plume emergency planning zone at the site boundary, justified by a mechanistic source term. The project budget and the site screen must still close if the NRC requires a conventional 10-mile zone. Do not select a site that only works under the optimistic zone.
• External hazards. Safe-shutdown earthquake at least 0.3 g horizontal, site-specific above that; flood above the coal plant’s historical basis plus a climate allowance; aircraft and vehicle barriers under 10 CFR 73. HALEU above 10 percent in formula quantities is special nuclear material of moderate strategic significance. Physical security is a cost line, not a brochure claim.

Beryllium toxicity and tritium are the two chemical issues that will draw intervenor attention. Both are manageable and neither is optional to analyze. Lithium-7 enrichment of the salt is the tritium control, backed by cover-gas capture. A beryllium hygiene program is an operating license exhibit.

8. Economics that can reach a credit committee
Capital is the product. On a light-water plant, fuel and operations are small beside the recovery of the build. US Forge-350 does not escape that. It tries to spend the capital on fewer unique civil works, a reactor that does not need a thick pressure vessel, and a site that does not need a new switchyard.

Case Overnight capital What it assumes U.S. AP1000 actual (Vogtle 3 and 4) $14,000–16,000/kW all-in Completed 2023–24; ~$31–37 billion for 2,234 MW
NuScale CFPP at cancellation, 2023 About  20,000/kW 462 MW estimate near $9.3 billion; project stopped
Natrium public target, Kemmerer About $11,000–12,000/kW Up to ~$4 billion for 345 MWe, about half DOE cost share BWRX-300 first unit, public TVA-range About $18,000/kW Figures near $5.4 billion before interest; later units hoped near $12,000/kW 
DOE nth-of-a-kind ambition About $3,600/kW overnight After 10–20 units; not a first-plant forecast
Forge-350 FOAK target $3.8–5.0 billion overnight $11,000–14,000/kW on 350 MWe firm; storage included
Forge-350 NOAK target, unit 8+ $2.0–2.6 billion overnight $6,000–7,500/kW on firm output, design frozen, coal site Figure. Capital anchors in public 2023–2026 figures, and Forge-350 planning bands. Overnight cost excludes interest during construction.

Interest is the second price. Five years of construction at 8 percent can add roughly a fifth to a quarter on top of overnight cost. That is why the schedule in Section 9 is a financial control, not a public-affairs date. A first unit at $4.4 billion overnight plus financing, running at 92 percent, needs on the order of $90–140 per megawatt-hour to cover capital alone before fuel, staff, and decommissioning, depending on the cost of money and the recovery period. Fuel and operations might add $15–25. Unassisted, that is not a merchant energy-only price. Assisted, it can be a contracted price.

The revenue stack that makes unit 1 bankable in the United States is specific:
• A long offtake from a utility, a federal power marketer, or a large load (data center or industrial host) covering at least 70 percent of firm output for 20 years or more. Merchant exposure on unit 1 is how projects die in the credit committee.
• A capacity payment on the storage-backed 150 MWe, sold separately from energy. This is the Natrium commercial idea, and it is worth more in a market that pays for accredited capacity than in an energy-only market.
• DOE cost share or a Title 17 loan guarantee on the first unit only. Kemmerer’s structure — public cost share on the order of half the FOAK premium — is the template. Later units should not need it, and the guide treats dependence on cost share past unit 2 as a kill signal.
• Tax position. New nuclear can qualify for the technology-neutral clean electricity production credit under section 45Y, or the investment credit under 48E, but not both on the same facility. With prevailing-wage and apprenticeship rules met, the production credit is on the order of 3 cents per kilowatt-hour after recent inflation adjustment (IRS notices for 2026 put the relevant alternative amount at 3.1 cents). A coal-closure energy community and domestic-content compliance can each add 10 percent. Full value for non-wind, non-solar technologies currently runs to facilities placed
in service by the end of 2033, with a partial window into 2035. Section 45U is for existing reactors placed in service before the Inflation Reduction Act, not for Forge-350. Confirm the window with tax counsel; do not build the model on a credit that expires before commercial operation.
At those supports, a plausible contracted price for unit 1 is $70–110 per megawatt-hour in levelized terms, falling toward $50–70 for a later unit if the NOAK band is hit. Those are planning ranges, not forecasts. The reader should notice that they overlap the real cost of firm gas plus a carbon or reliability constraint, and that they do not overlap unsubsidized energy-only solar.

9. Implementation guide:

The sequence below is written for an owner who does not yet have a site. Elapsed time from a serious start to commercial  operation is eight to ten years if fuel and the test reactor cooperate, and longer if they do not. The 2026 permit reviews — about fourteen months for TVA’s BWRX-300 application, and under two years from docketing to permit for Natrium — are the new benchmark. They are not a promise. 

Gate When Exit criteria — do not pass without these
0 Owner Month 0–6 Taxable owner, state partner, and a balance sheet that can carry $50–100 million of development cost.

Joint venture acceptable; a shell company is not.

1 Site and offtake Month 3–18 Two coal or brownfield sites under option. Interconnection position. Offtake term sheet for ≥70% of firm output. Water and transmission fatal-flaw screen.

2 Fuel Month 6–18, before CP file HALEU allocation or commercial enrichment contract, and a fabrication slot. If neither can be dated, switch the nuclear island to the light-water off-ramp.

3 Pre-application Month 6–24 NRC engagement plan, white papers on functional containment, salt spill, pebble handling, and EPZ.

ASME code-case plan. Owner’s engineer appointed.

4 Construction permit File ~month 24; review 14–24 
months PSAR, environmental report, safeguards. Limited work authorization for non-nuclear work. Hearing strategy budgeted.

5 FID and build Month 42–90 Overnight cost band reconfirmed. EPC is multi-contract or has a replaceable nuclear constructor.

Non-nuclear complete. Fuel delivery date inside the outage window.

6 Operating license In parallel with build FSAR, technical specifications, emergency plan, security plan, beryllium and tritium programs.

ITAAC-equivalent closure.

7 Commercial Month 96–120 Power ascension, warranty run, offtake conversion. NOAK design freeze within 12 months of commercial operation, or the fleet does not get cheaper.

Figure. Decision gates. A missed fuel gate switches technology. It does not slip the site.

9.1 Contracting:
Vogtle concentrated risk in a consortium that could not absorb it. Kemmerer’s 2026 EPC split showed the same
single-point exposure on an advanced reactor. Forge-350 should be bid as packages: nuclear island, salt systems, turbine island, civil, and integration. The owner keeps an owner’s engineer with stop-work authority. Liquidated damages are worth less than the right to retender a package. Fixed-price on a finished design is reasonable for units 3 and after. Fixed-price on unit 1 is how contractors put contingency in the number or walk away when the number is wrong.

9.2 Light-water off-ramp:
At Gate 2 and again at Gate 4, the owner scores HALEU delivery, TRISO qualification, and Flibe supply as red, amber, or green. Two reds switch the nuclear island to a licensed light-water SMR on the same site, same offtake, and same interconnection — the BWRX-300 being the design with a U.S. construction permit and a Canadian lead unit. The storage tanks can still be installed and charged electrically or from a later salt unit. The off-ramp is a feature. A project that cannot
abandon its favorite coolant is a project that will wait past the tax window.

9.3 Fleet, not a single plaque:
Unit 1 is a demonstration that happens to sell power. Units 3 through 8 are the product. The implementation plan should name eight coal sites in two reliability regions before unit 1 pours nuclear concrete, even if only two are under option.  Design changes after unit 1 commercial operation require a written reason. Every “improvement” that breaks serial fabrication is presumed rejected. This is the Korean and Chinese lesson that survives translation: the second unit is cheaper only if it is the same unit.

10. Regulatory path:
File unit 1 under 10 CFR Part 50: construction permit, then operating license. That is the path Natrium and the Clinch River BWRX-300 actually used. Part 52 design certification is the right step for unit 3, once the as-built design has stopped moving. Part 53, when it is final and the staff has reviewed one application under it, can become the fleet path. Leading with an unfinished rule is how a project becomes the staff’s learning case.
• Pre-application: topical reports on TRISO in salt (building on KP-BISON), Flibe chemistry, confinement versus containment, and a proposed principal design criteria set aligned with the NRC’s advanced-reactor design criteria.
• Environmental report: coal-site reuse is the mitigation story — no new transmission corridor, reuse of intake where legal, remediation overlap with coal ash only if the plume interaction is actually analyzed. NEPA delay is a schedule risk equal to the safety review.
• Hearings: the ADVANCE Act and later bills have moved some uncontested hearing practice. Contested hearings have not been abolished. Budget 12 to 18 months of hearing time in the permit float rather than discovering it at the end.
• State: a certificate of public convenience and necessity or equivalent, water permit, air permit for auxiliary boilers and cooling towers, and a state emergency-planning agreement. A federal construction permit without a state certificate is not a start of construction.
• Security and material: Category II physical protection if HALEU quantities require it; transport packages for fresh pebbles and spent pebbles licensed before the first shipment, not before the first outage.
Price-Anderson indemnity applies to a licensed plant and should be confirmed in the ownership agreement so a minority investor is not surprised by the channeling of liability. Decommissioning funding starts with a site-specific estimate at operating-license stage and a trust funded under the NRC’s formula. Salt inventory disposition is part of that estimate; it is not free.
11. Supply chain that must exist before concrete
A reader who remembers only one list should remember this one. Each line has killed or slipped a real project.
• HALEU enrichment. Pilot kilograms at Piketon do not fill an 830 MWt core. Contract tonnes, with a second source or a DOE backstop, before the construction-permit filing.
• TRISO fabrication. One Part 70 license exists. A second shop, or a qualified second line in the first shop, is the difference between a fleet and a prototype.
• Nuclear graphite. Qualify the actual billet supplier. Substitution after the permit is a license amendment.
• Lithium-7 and beryllium. Flibe is not a catalog chemical at reactor purity. Lead time is measured in years. Beryllium handling is a siting constraint for the fabrication shop as well as the plant.
• High-temperature code materials. Open the ASME cases during pre-application. An unqualified alloy is a redesign.
• Nitrate-salt tanks and heat tracing. Buy the solar-thermal lessons, including the failures. Freeze-up is a plant trip, and a dirty freeze-up is a multi-month outage.
• Turbine and generator. A 350–500 MWe supercritical set is a commercial machine. Order it when the offtake is signed; it is no longer the long pole if the salt systems are real.
• Operators. A coal workforce transfers maintenance culture, not licensed-operator qualifications. The senior reactor operator pipeline starts at Gate 3, not at fuel load.
12. Risk register and kill criteria
Risk What it does to the project Kill or mitigate
HALEU not available in tonnes by Gate 4 Moves commercial operation past the 45Y window Kill the salt island; take the light-water off-ramp TRISO-in-salt data do not support the source term

Forces a conventional containment and a new cost Redesign only if overnight cost stays inside the FOAK band; else off-ramp:

Single EPC dispute 2026 Kemmerer lesson; months vanish in rebidding Multi-package contracts; replaceable constructor Interest during a slip past 6 years Adds more cost than any efficiency gain removes FID only with fuel date, permit, and offtake; no speculative start Contested hearing on EPZ or beryllium 12–24 month delay Site works under a 10-mile EPZ; hygiene program in the application

Salt freeze or tank leak Long outage after commercial operation Drain design, tracing, and a spare tank nozzle strategy in the bid Cost share promised but not appropriated FOAK capital hole FID condition precedent: executed DOE agreement, not a press 
release.

Risk:
What it does to the project Kill or mitigate
Design changes after unit 1 NOAK never arrives Change board; serial-fabrication presumption figure. Risks that stop the project, as distinct from risks that merely need a procedure.
13. A twenty-four-month checklist for the reader
The guide is written so that a utility planner, a state energy office, or an investor can act without waiting for a vendor’s brochure. The first two years are development, not construction.
• Name the owner. If the reader is a state office, pick the public-power or cooperative counterparty that can hold a license. The NRC licenses a person, not a concept.
• Screen retiring coal units for interconnection, land, flood, seismic category, and community position. Drop any site that only works with a reduced emergency planning zone.
• Ask the offtaker for a term sheet, not a memorandum. Data-center load is real only when the ramp and the curtailment terms are written down.
• Open a fuel dialogue with DOE’s HALEU program and with the licensed fabricator in the same quarter. Track
kilograms under contract, not announcements.
• Fund an owner’s engineer to produce a site-specific overnight cost with a −20 / +40 percent FOAK band. Reject any estimate shown as a single number.
• Request an NRC pre-application meeting only after the site shortlist and the fuel path exist. A meeting with neither wastes the staff’s calendar and the owner’s credibility.
• Model 45Y and 48E as sensitivities, including a case with no credit. If the no-credit case cannot be carried by the offtake, the project needs cost share or it needs to wait for unit 3 of somebody else’s design.
• Write the off-ramp into the partnership agreement so a technology switch does not require a unanimous consent that will never come.
• Engage the coal plant’s operators and the nearest nuclear plant’s training pipeline. The license will be won or lost on people as much as on salt.
• Publish the kill criteria. A project that cannot say what would stop it is asking its ratepayers for a blank check — the error Vogtle made legible.
14. Sources and limits:
Operating-fleet capacity factor (91 percent in 2025) and fleet size (94 reactors, about 97 GW) are from EIA-based public summaries. Vogtle cost and schedule are from owner filings and contemporary reporting, which do not agree on a single dollar figure; this guide uses the $31–37 billion, $14,000–16,000 per kilowatt band. Natrium’s construction permit (March 2026), 345 / 500 MWe rating, and DOE cost share are from NRC and DOE releases; the Bechtel EPC exit is from September 2026 trade reporting. TVA’s Clinch River BWRX-300 construction permit is from the NRC action of 29
September 2026. Hermes temperatures, power, Flibe coolant, and TRISO fuel are from the Kairos preliminary safety analysis report on the NRC docket and from the applicant’s public descriptions. HALEU licensing status is from the NRC’s public HALEU page. Tax credit structure is from 26 U.S.C. §§ 45U and 45Y and from 2026 IRS inflation notices; eligibility windows have already been amended once and should be re-read before a financial close.
What this guide does not do: it does not size a core, it does not calculate a source term, and it does not replace a vendor safety analysis. Forge-350 is the architecture the 2026 record supports — solid fuel, low pressure, coal-site wires, storage sold as capacity, a permit path the NRC has just shown it can finish, and a fuel gate that is allowed to say no. The plant gets
built, if it gets built, by an owner who keeps those constraints tighter than the technology story.
15. Decision card:
Use this card in a resource-planning or investment meeting. It is the guide compressed to the choices that change a go / no-go, not a substitute for the sections above.

Question Answer this guide supports:
What should unit 1 be? 
One 830 MWt Flibe-cooled TRISO module, 350 MWe firm, 500 MWe for five hours from nitrate-salt storage, on a retiring coal site.
Why not an AP1000? Best safety maturity, worst recent U.S. cost. A second pair only makes sense on a frozen design with a warm supply chain — not as the efficiency or schedule fix.

Why not start with BWRX-300? Start there if HALEU is red at Gate 2. Otherwise hold it as the off-ramp. It is licensable now and thermally inefficient.
Why not Natrium as specified? Copy the storage split and the coal site. Do not copy sodium for a first fleet if Flibe can carry the same heat without a sodium-water
reaction.

Why not liquid thorium? Best long-run fuel story, no U.S. construction-permit precedent, no commercial salt-fuel plant. A 2040s program, not a 2030s resource plan.

What permit? 10 CFR 50 construction permit, then operating license. Part 52 after the design freezes. Part 53 only once the staff has used it.

What has to be signed before filing? Offtake term sheet for at least 70 percent of firm output, a dated HALEU and TRISO path, and an owner’s engineer cost band — not a single number.

What kills the salt plant? No tonnes of HALEU by Gate 4, a source term that forces a new containment outside the cost band, or cost share that exists only as a 
press release.

What does success look like? Unit 1 commercial in the mid-2030s inside the FOAK band, and a frozen design copied onto named coal sites without a new coolant.
Bottom line for the reader. Do not wait for a perfect reactor. File a low-pressure, TRISO-fueled module on a coal site, with storage on the intermediate loop, under a Part 50 construction permit, and with a signed HALEU path. If the fuel path fails, build the light-water plant the same site was screened for. Serial copies, not a new coolant every five years, are what move U.S. nuclear off the Vogtle cost curve.

The One-Third Rule: your landed cost has to be one third of your price or less, and one quarter is better.

Landed cost means everything it takes to get the product to the customer's door. The unit, the packaging, the freight and the shipping, not just what the factory quotes you.

This matters more than any ad you'll ever find. Every customer you buy on Meta costs roughly what it costs your competitors, because you're all in the same auction. 

The only thing you control is how much is left after the product is paid for. At one third, a $60 order leaves you $40 to buy the customer and still make money. At one half, it leaves you $30, and the first time CPMs jump in Q4 you're paying to sell.

Most founders find this out at scale. They find a winner, push budget, and end the month with a big revenue screenshot and nothing in the bank, because every new sale scaled a margin that was too thin from day one.

So before I look at a single ad for a new product, I check 3 things:
1. Landed cost with shipping, not the factory price
2. The price the market already pays for it
3. Whether a bundle or a subscription can push the math further in my favor

If the product fails the One-Third Rule, no creative will save it. Fix the math first, then scale.

text:
The debate surrounding #Starlink in #India is not really about internet speeds, rural connectivity or even Elon Musk.

It is about #sovereignty 
History teaches us that nations rarely lose strategic autonomy overnight. More often, dependence develops gradually through systems, networks and institutions that become too important to function without.

The #BritishEastIndiaCompany did not arrive in India as a conquering army. It arrived as a commercial enterprise promising trade, access to global markets and economic opportunity. Over time, commercial influence evolved into political leverage, strategic control and eventually colonial rule.

The world of the 21st century is different, but the underlying principle remains relevant.

Today, influence is exercised not only through territory and military power but through data, communications infrastructure, digital platforms, satellite networks and technological dependence.

This is where Starlink becomes a strategic question rather than merely a telecommunications project.

Supporters correctly point out that satellite internet can transform connectivity in remote regions, improve disaster response and bridge digital divides. These are real benefits.

However, strategic planners must also ask a different set of questions:
“Who controls the network?
Who ultimately decides where service is available?”

What happens during a geopolitical crisis?
Can a sovereign nation guarantee uninterrupted access if the infrastructure is owned, operated and controlled by a foreign private entity?

The Ukraine conflict offers a powerful example.
Reports revealed that Starlink services were restricted during a planned Ukrainian operation targeting Russian naval assets near Crimea. The result was that the operation could not proceed as intended because the communications network required for execution was unavailable.

Regardless of one’s views on the decision, the larger geopolitical lesson is clear:
A private company and its leadership possessed the ability to influence the operational options available to a sovereign state during an active conflict.

That reality should concern every serious strategic planner in the world.
The issue is not whether Elon Musk was right or wrong.

The issue is whether any nation should place critical national communications infrastructure in a position where ultimate operational control rests outside its sovereign authority.

For India, this question carries even greater significance.

India faces an increasingly contested security environment stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. #Communications resilience is not merely an economic requirement; it is a #nationalsecurity necessity.

This does not mean rejecting foreign technology.
India has benefited enormously from international investment, technology partnerships and global integration.

But integration should never become dependence.
The ideal outcome is not isolation but strategic balance: encouraging innovation while ensuring robust regulatory oversight, #dataprotection, local compliance requirements and #sovereigncontrol mechanisms.

The lesson of the #EastIndiaCompany is often misunderstood.
The danger was never trade itself.

The danger was allowing critical leverage to accumulate outside Indian control.

As technology becomes the new arena of geopolitical competition, nations must remember a simple principle:
Infrastructure creates dependence.
Dependence creates leverage.
Leverage creates influence.

And influence, if left unchecked, can eventually challenge sovereignty itself.

India was colonised once through commerce and influence.
The next challenge, if it ever comes, will not arrive on sailing ships.

It will arrive through networks, platforms, satellites and systems that become too important to question

That is why the Starlink debate is not merely abt connectivity.
It is about ensuring that 🇮🇳’s digital future remains firmly under Indian sovereign control #JaiHind

text:
Global Access Map: Where Starlink is Blocked or Awaiting Approval
While SpaceX’s Starlink now operates in over 100 countries, significant global coverage gaps remain due to geopolitical sanctions, state security policies, and pending spectrum licenses.
1. Restricted & State-Banned Nations
(Blocked due to state monopolies, security restrictions, or international sanctions)
 * China: Banned to protect domestic space and satellite constellations (Guowang / Qianfan).
 * Russia: Banned due to national security concerns and military restrictions.
 * Iran: Blocked locally under strict state internet control and US sanctions.
 * North Korea: Total state-enforced telecommunications blackout.
 * Syria: Under comprehensive international sanctions and state regulatory blocks.
 * Cuba: Restricted under US embargo provisions and state telecommunications law.
 * Belarus: Blocked under regional security arrangements and active sanctions.
 * Afghanistan: Unapproved under current administrative and telecommunications rules.
 * Myanmar: Banned by the military regime, with strict prohibitions on satellite hardware.
 * Venezuela: Lacks operational authorization and regulatory agreements.
2. Pending Regulatory & Spectrum Approvals
(Applications submitted or trials underway, awaiting final commercial clearance)
 * India: Awaiting finalized administrative spectrum allocations, pricing, and national security clearances.
 * South Africa: Held up by the mandatory 30% local equity ownership rule for telecom operators.
 * Pakistan: Pending technical and security evaluation by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA).
 * Vietnam: Subject to mandatory local data storage and joint-venture corporate requirements.
 * Thailand: Under review by the NBTC regarding foreign satellite licensing guidelines.
 * Turkey: Pending national spectrum assignment and BTK regulatory approval.
 * Saudi Arabia: Ongoing discussions covering CITC licensing and localized infrastructure.
 * UAE: Commercial satellite broadband applications currently under review by TDRA.
 * Bangladesh: Technical trials completed; awaiting final spectrum license terms.
 * Egypt: Subject to military and national telecom regulatory agency approvals.
3. Regulatory Crackdowns on Grey-Market Imports
In several markets without direct licenses (notably Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Sudan, and Namibia), local telecom authorities have penalized the illicit importation of roaming terminals, prompting SpaceX to enforce geofencing until commercial licenses are granted.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

My boyfriend asked me to delete one contact from my phone. I did. The next morning, that same number called me.
It happened on a Sunday night.

My boyfriend, Daniel, was sitting beside me on the couch when he suddenly asked:

“Who is Michael?”

I looked at him, confused.
“Michael who?”

He picked up my phone and showed me a contact I barely remembered saving.

Michael.

I laughed.

“He's nobody. I think that's an old contact.”

Daniel didn't laugh.

“Delete it.”

I stared at him.

“Why?”

“Just delete it.”

The way he said it made me uncomfortable.
I asked him how he knew about Michael, but he avoided the question.

Instead, he said:
“If you trust me, delete the number.”

I didn't want to argue, so I deleted it.

Then I showed him my recently deleted contacts.
He watched carefully until he was sure it was gone.

“Good,” he said.

I thought that was the end of it.

Until the next morning.
At exactly 7:14 AM, my phone rang.

I looked at the screen.

Unknown Number.

I answered.
“Hello?” 

There was silence.

Then a man's voice whispered:
“Why did you delete my number?”

My heart stopped.
Because I recognized the voice.
It was Michael.

The same man Daniel had just told me to delete.

And then Michael said something that made me realize Daniel had lied to me about something.

“Your boyfriend knows exactly who I am.”

Daniel had snatched the phone from my hand and smashed it against the wall.

You were never supposed to remember him.

"Daniel, what are you talking about? Remember who?"

Inside were printed screenshots. Old Facebook messages. Police reports.

My brother, Kofi, didn't die in a car accident in 2021.

A fight with Daniel.

Daniel was his friend. They fought over money Daniel owed him. Daniel pushed him. Kofi fell and hit his head. Daniel left him there.

Michael was the only witness. Daniel begged him to stay quiet and paid him off. He made Michael promise to never contact my family again.

That's why when Daniel saw "Michael" on my phone — my brother's best friend — he panicked. He knew if I ever talked to Michael, the truth about my brother would come out.

I walked back inside.

Daniel was on his knees, crying.

Sometimes God uses the contact you almost deleted to reveal the devil sleeping next to you.

*THE END.*

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
A road safety officer stopped us today. My brother was driving, and he presented his valid UAE/Dubai driving licence. The vehicle papers were checked everything was intact. Fire extinguisher? Intact. Warning triangle? Intact. Spare tyre? Intact.

The officer then demanded a Nigerian driver's licence. My brother explained that we don't reside in Nigeria and had only just returned. The officer insisted that a Dubai licence could not be used in Nigeria, even for one day.

I simply asked him to show us the specific law we had violated. Instead of showing the law, the attitude changed. He started saying I was claiming to know everything and that "this is Nigeria."

I also explained that my own Nigerian driver's licence has expired because I no longer drive in Nigeria. I told him I have not driven since I returned and have no intention of renewing a licence for a vehicle I am not driving. He insisted that even if I don't drive, I must renew it.

I asked him: Why should I keep spending money renewing a driver's licence when I have decided not to drive in Nigeria? And why are citizens constantly being suffocated with one charge, renewal or demand after another?

I even asked whether he understood that citizens have constitutional rights and should not be treated as if every interaction with a government officer must end in intimidation or payment. He simply looked at me as though I was the one who had lost my mind.

What made it worse was seeing a condemned truck that clearly should not have been on the road pass right in front of us without being stopped, while we were being held over a valid foreign driver's licence.

When I questioned the double standard, the situation escalated. I made a phone call, and the officer accused me of calling "cultists" to attack them.

The next thing, a JTF team comprising soldiers, police and civil defence arrived aggressively, shouting for everyone to come down from the vehicle. We were three people—my brother, his wife and me. His wife was still inside the vehicle.

They aggressively tried to take my phone when I was recording what was happening. I asked them to first hear our side of the story.

After they eventually listened and confirmed what had happened, we were told to leave and not be aggressive towards officers. But I never came there looking for trouble. I was simply asking questions and trying to document what was happening to us.

They later insisted that I delete the video, which I did in their presence.

Why all this suffocation of citizens?

Why must asking a legitimate question to a government officer suddenly become "insulting an officer," "knowing too much," or "challenging authority"?

Respect for citizens and respect for personnel must work both ways. A uniform is not a licence to intimidate citizens, and citizens should not have to surrender their rights simply because someone in uniform says, "This is Nigeria."

Say NO to citizens' intimidation.

I will never bow to intimidation or oppression.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
Why should we not stay in India anymore?

I recently had a terrifying experience on the night of 25th September 2026 during Ganesh Utsav, that I feel compelled to share it.

While attending the Utsav, my iPhone was stolen from my pocket near Nagarkar Talim Chowk on Laxmi Road at around 10:30 PM IST. I was alert, and the moment it was taken, I immediately realized that someone had removed it from my pocket. I checked with the people around me, but the phone was already gone.

I immediately rushed to the nearest police station, Vishrambaug Police Station, where I filed an FIR. After getting a duplicate SIM card issued, I also had my IMEI number blocked.

However, I did not lose hope. I continued trying to find ways to track my device on my own. As part of this effort, I even visited several police stations to check whether they had caught any thieves from whom my phone might have been recovered. Unfortunately, I had no luck.

Then, while all of this was going on, I received two SMS messages on my registered number from the thief. The messages claimed that my phone had been located and provided a link supposedly allowing me to track its location. I immediately recognized it as a phishing attempt.

I went to the nearest police station to report this, hoping that this new information might actually help track the person who had stolen my phone. Instead, I was told to go back to the police station where I had originally filed my FIR.

So I went back to Vishrambaug Police Station. They gave me the numbers of two police officers and asked me to contact them. I did exactly that. But after explaining the entire situation, I was told the same thing I already knew: “This is a fake link. Don’t click on it.”

And that was it.

No further assistance. No attempt to investigate the phone number. No effort to use the information I had provided. Nothing…

I thought about it for a while and realized that perhaps the Maharashtra Cyber Police could help. I had the thief's phone number, and I assumed that a cyber crime department would have the necessary resources and technology to trace the number and potentially locate the device or identify the person behind it.

So I traveled to Shivajinagar, where the Maharashtra Cyber Police headquarters are located. There, I was told to contact the Rural Cyber Police because I live in a rural area.

I then traveled to the Rural Cyber Cell. And guess what I was told there? “Your FIR is with Pune Police, so you need to check with them.”

At this point, I had gone from one police station to another, from one department to another, carrying the same information and explaining the same situation repeatedly.

And after going through all of this, I realized just how helpless an ordinary taxpayer can feel when they actually need the system to work. I have paid taxes for years. I have followed the law. I did exactly what a responsible citizen is supposed to do, yet when I actually needed assistance, there was no coordination.

One department directed me to another. One police station directed me to another. Officials repeated information that I already knew instead of acting on the new information I was providing. There appeared to be no clear ownership of the case and no one willing to take responsibility for actually pursuing it.
What is the point of filing an FIR and registering on CEIR portal, when new and potentially useful information emerges, the victim is simply sent from one department to another?

And where is the technology that should allow law enforcement to act quickly in cases like this?
The most frustrating part is that I wasn't asking anyone to perform a miracle. I wasn't asking for special treatment. I was asking for basic assistance after becoming a victim of a crime.

Instead, I spent my time travelling between police stations, departments and offices, repeatedly explaining the same situation, while everyone seemed more interested in telling me who was not responsible rather than figuring out who was.

This experience has left me extremely disappointed and angry.

A common taxpayer should not have to become an investigator, case coordinator and police liaison just to get basic assistance after their phone is stolen. If this is what a citizen has to go through even after immediately reporting a crime and providing potentially useful information, then something is seriously wrong with the system.

I understood if any important person's son or daughter phone would have been stolen in the same way, these department would have worked very differently and the phone would probably be recovered within days but unfortunately we are just a common middle class man who does have any power nor have anyone's help. We are just money printing machine for the Indian government.

Dealing this situation made me realized how bad India is, why we should not stay in this country.

@mohol_murlidhar @MDNagpure @SunetraA_Pawar  @CPPuneCity @PuneCityPolice @mieknathshinde @Dev_Fadnavis @PMOIndia 
 
#consumerProtection #UnfairPolicies #ConsumerRights

text:
The Pothole Is Not an Accident

On the morning of Saturday, 13 June 2026, a woman named Kantha was riding her two-wheeler along the Siddapur road near Marathahalli, dropping her daughter Neha at college. It had rained heavily the night before, and the potholes had filled with water, which is the detail that makes them invisible. She hit one, lost control and fell. A school bus coming from behind ran her over. She died on the road, in front of her daughter.

A case was registered at the Whitefield traffic police station. Against the bus.

That is the whole architecture of the problem in one line. There is always a vehicle to charge. There is never a road to charge.

Kantha's death was not a freak event. In Bengaluru it is closer to a season. The National Crime Records Bureau counts deaths caused by the negligence of civic bodies, meaning bad roads, potholes, open drains, collapsing infrastructure, electrocution. Bengaluru has ranked first among Indian metros in that category for six consecutive years. Delhi, bigger and denser and not famous for good roads, recorded four in a year when Bengaluru recorded seventeen. Either Bengaluru's roads are uniquely lethal, or every other city is better at not counting.

The national picture, in passing: figures tabled in Parliament record 9,438 people killed in pothole crashes between 2020 and 2024, about five a day, the toll rising 53% across those years. The Supreme Court called such numbers frightening as far back as 2018. Yet the same table shows Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Goa reporting zero pothole deaths in five years. Not zero potholes. Zero deaths. That is not a measurement. It is a filing decision.

A pothole death exists, legally, only if a police officer writes the word pothole into an FIR. Most do not. The crash becomes rash driving, or a hit-and-run. There is a driver to arrest and a section of the penal code that fits him. There is no section that fits an engineer who certified a road that dissolved in the first monsoon.

Bengaluru has a case that shows exactly how that works. On 6 February 2021, Tasdeeq Bushra, nineteen and in her first year of MBBS, was riding home along Hennur Main Road. She swerved to avoid a pothole. A truck hit her scooter from behind, she fell, and she went under the wheels.

The truck belonged to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike. The city's own civic body owned the vehicle that killed her, and the road, and the pothole she was avoiding. The driver was arrested under Section 304A, causing death by negligence. The agency was not. Her father, Mushtaq Ahmed, put it better than any court has: "We have lost our only child. Whom will we pin the blame on? The vehicle was BBMP's and so was the driver, the roads were poorly built by them." BBMP, the water board and the electricity utility then blamed one another, which is the standard procedure.

Two details from what followed are worth sitting with. The FIR did not mention the pothole. And the pothole was filled within hours of her death. The evidence was repaired faster than the case was built.

Hers is not an outlier, it is the template. The News Minute traced thirteen pothole deaths in Bengaluru between 2017 and 2022. Families compensated: zero. Officials held accountable: zero. Not for want of a policy. BBMP had notified one, three lakh rupees for a death, and reporters found zonal chief engineers who did not know it existed and had never received a claim. A right nobody is told about is not a right, it is a press release. When Ashwin, twenty-seven, died on a pothole in MS Palya, police first blamed him for riding irresponsibly. His mother fought to get one line into the FIR naming unnamed civic officers. Nothing came of it.

The courts have been trying for a decade. A petition filed in 2015 is still running, and the High Court has reprimanded the corporation repeatedly, once issuing a contempt notice after BBMP resisted paying compensation at all. At one hearing, BBMP informed the court that Bengaluru contained 221 potholes in total. The court told it to be honest.

Then came the deadline. After a student named Dhanushree was crushed by a tipper lorry in September 2025 while swerving around a pothole, the Chief Minister announced that Bengaluru would be pothole-free by the end of October, with eleven hundred crore rupees sanctioned. Officials counted potholes by the thousand and announced them filled. The deadline was missed and replaced with another. In Whitefield, residents watched gravel tipped into holes, gravel that scatters as soon as vehicles pass over it.

Here is how that pothole-free year ended. On 20 November, three weeks after the deadline, Shantamma, forty-six, riding pillion home from work, fell on a broken stretch in Hulimavu and was run over by a truck. Police blamed potholes and loose gravel. On 17 December, Tabrez, thirty-two, swerved near Nelamangala and put his front wheel into an unbarricaded pipeline pit. He died at NIMHANS two days later. Not a pothole, strictly. The same disease.

Then the rains came back in June, and so did the holes, and so did Kantha's funeral.

The exhausting part is that the effort is real. The money is spent, the holes are counted and announced, and they return on schedule, because filling a pothole is not building a road. A pothole is the visible end of a chain: a specification diluted, a layer skipped, a bill cleared, an inspection signed. Every hole in a Bengaluru road has a name attached to it somewhere. None of those names ever reaches an FIR.

A drunk driver goes to jail. A negligent engineer gets transferred. A contractor whose road failed in ten weeks bids for the next tender. The person who dies becomes a line in a table.

Bengaluru has led that table for six years and has still not produced one official who lost a job over a death. Until a road failure is something a person can be charged with, the ritual continues: a monsoon, a hole, a two-wheeler, a bus behind it, a case against the driver, gravel by the weekend, and a family being told that what happened to them was an accident.

It was not an accident. Someone built that.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.
